name: The Longfellow Linden

location.address: Longfellow House-Washington's Headquarters National Historic Site, 105 Brattle Street, Cambridge, MA
location.neighbourhood: Cambridge (within the day-trip boundary of Boston, roughly 20-25 minutes via Red Line to Harvard Square then a short walk)

access: Free; National Historic Site grounds are open to the public daily during daylight hours (house tours are separately ticketed but the East Lawn where the tree stands is publicly accessible)
transport: MBTA Red Line to Harvard Square, then about 8-10 minutes on foot down Brattle Street
verify_notes: Planted around 1800-1810 by Andrew Craigie, who owned the estate before Henry Wadsworth Longfellow acquired it in 1843; NPS dates it to 'approximately 200 years' as of its plant-story writeup (source undated but recent), and a 2018 Cambridge tree blog independently calls it '200+ years old, 110 feet high'. Longfellow himself wrote about the tree in his journal: distraught in summer 1844 when workmen 'lopped away the long low branches of my Linden tree, misunderstanding my directions' ('O day of woe! My walk on the Eastern piazza is desecrated!'), and by 1846 describing his wife Fanny reading Heine's poetry beneath its branches. Fanny Longfellow wrote in 1843 of hoping for 'a linden avenue in which my poet intends to pace in his old age & compose under its shade' -- this surviving tree is the only one of that planned avenue left. Stands on the East Lawn beside the house. Alive today but condition rated 'fair to poor' by NPS: a filled trunk cavity and cables stabilize branches; NPS runs a 5-year heavy-pruning maintenance cycle and started a propagation program in the early 2000s to grow a genetically identical successor for eventual succession, which is itself evidence the park considers the original tree at end-of-life risk but currently standing and actively maintained, not dead. Measurements per NPS: 82 feet tall (species average is ~60 ft), 84 inches DBH, 40 ft canopy spread. Location set to 'approximate': coordinates given are for the historic site/house itself (105 Brattle St), not a surveyed tree-level GPS point; the tree stands on the East Lawn adjacent to the house, which anyone visiting the grounds will find easily, but I could not confirm an exact lat/long for the trunk itself. Two of the three sources cited (NPS interpretive article, and a landscape-preservation blog affiliated with the NPS Olmsted Center) both trace back to National Park Service documentation of the site; the third (Empty Mass Ave, an independent Cambridge blog) is genuinely independent and corroborates age, height and 'alive today' status. Flagging curation_status because the two NPS-linked sources are not fully independent of each other, even though the facts are consistent and well documented (the National Park Service's own Cultural Landscape Report for this site exists as a fourth, more technical source but is a scanned PDF with no extractable text in the time available this pass).

name: The Houghton Beech

location.address: 1000-1008 Massachusetts Avenue, Cambridge, MA (between Harvard Square and Central Square, on the site of the former Houghton estate, now part of MIT/University Park land)
location.neighbourhood: Cambridge, Mid-Cambridge/University Park (within the day-trip boundary; on the Red Line corridor)

access: Free; stands beside a public sidewalk on Massachusetts Avenue, fully visible and reachable at any time
transport: MBTA Red Line to Central Square, then about 8 minutes on foot along Mass Ave toward Harvard Square
verify_notes: Cambridge's only living Historic Landmark, designated by the Cambridge Historical Commission in 1985 specifically to save this tree: a developer's planned office building would have destroyed a third of its crown and killed it outright, and a resident group called 'Friends of the Beech Tree' (about 30 people) petitioned the city to intervene. The Harvard Crimson, reporting live on the October 1985 landmark hearing, gives the tree's age at that time as '203-year-old', which would place planting around 1782 (note: the same Crimson piece states Henry Houghton 'served as mayor in 1782', which is almost certainly a transcription/OCR slip for a later 19th-century mayoral term, since Houghton founded Houghton Mifflin/Riverside Press decades later; the planting-year math from the stated age is more reliable than that specific biographical detail, so age_min/max is centered on the 203-year 1985 figure carried forward to 2026, i.e. roughly 244 years, rounded to 'roughly 240 years'). A 2018 independent Cambridge tree blog (Empty Mass Ave) separately describes it as 'planted 150+ years ago', a looser, rounder estimate that is a lower bound rather than a contradiction (150+ is consistent with 240). Species is copper/purple beech, a cultivar of European beech. It is the sole survivor of three beech trees Henry O. Houghton originally planted on his family estate; the estate's buildings were demolished when MIT acquired the property in the 1970s, but the tree itself was spared and later legally protected. The Cambridge Historical Commission's own landmark designation report (official government record) exists as a fourth source at the URL above but is a scanned image PDF with no extractable text layer in the time available this pass (note for the fetch-blocklist: cambridgema.gov landmark-report PDFs under /historicalcommission/pdf/Landmark_reports/ are scanned images, no OCR text layer). Location set to 'approximate': address and neighbourhood are well documented (1000-1008 Mass Ave, across from where the Orson Welles Cinema once stood, now University Park), but I do not have a surveyed tree-level GPS point, only a street-address-level location. Flagging curation_status for the same reason as bos_009: strong facts, but the numeric age comes from a single 1985 newspaper figure rather than two fully independent measurements, even though a second source (Empty Mass Ave) and the fact of an official 1985 government landmark designation both corroborate that this is a genuinely old, well-documented, legally protected individual tree.
